india.why: The important change from yesterday is operational preparedness. Rainfall, coastal exposure and landslide risk require different local responses; a state-wide headline cannot tell a particular household which route or shelter is safe.
india.soWhat: People with coastal travel, fishing activity or scheduled deliveries should verify district instructions and operator notices before departure.
india.take: I would act on official local warnings now rather than interpret uncertainty as safety.

india.why: Consumption and government investment can support activity while expensive energy and borrowing squeeze household budgets. A strong aggregate result can therefore coexist with stress among agriculture-dependent families and interest-sensitive businesses.
india.soWhat: For planning, test demand assumptions against sector orders, employment and collections rather than treating the headline forecast as uniform prosperity.
india.take: I would use the poll as a baseline scenario, with room for substantial revision.

tech.why: Financial agents can combine sensitive data with permissions to take consequential actions. Assurance therefore needs to test tool boundaries, failure recovery and traceability, alongside the model’s ability to answer questions correctly.
tech.soWhat: Banks, insurers and fintech teams can use this agenda to structure procurement questions and request reproducible test evidence.
tech.take: I would welcome a shared testing capability while waiting for published methods and results.
tech.watch: Named institutional participation, released evaluation protocols and independently reproducible findings will demonstrate progress.

psychology.label: Psychology · 19 Nov 2026
psychology.headline: A unanimous room can make an obvious answer feel wrong
psychology.summary: Solomon Asch’s 1956 report studied 123 male college students judging line lengths while confederates deliberately gave wrong answers. Participants sometimes followed the unanimous majority despite an objectively clear task. This classic laboratory result concerns social pressure; it does not establish that every group or culture behaves identically.
psychology.why: Public disagreement can carry a social cost even when private evidence looks clear. Independent judgments become harder once everyone hears the same confident answer.
psychology.soWhat: Collect initial estimates privately before a workplace review, particularly when senior colleagues speak first.
psychology.take: Independent estimates are worth protecting before a confident majority forms.
psychology.watch: Compare the spread of anonymous initial estimates with the final group judgment at your next review.

psychology.label: Psychology · 19 Nov 2026
psychology.headline: Authority needs explicit limits before pressure arrives
psychology.summary: Stanley Milgram’s 1963 obedience experiment recruited 40 men aged 20–50. Participants believed they were delivering escalating electric shocks under an experimenter’s direction; the learner actually received none. Many continued despite visible distress. Deception and participant stress make the study ethically contested, and its narrow sample limits generalisation.
psychology.why: Legitimate roles and incremental instructions can make responsibility feel transferred upward. Situational pressure is therefore worth addressing through procedures rather than assuming good intentions will always suffice.
psychology.soWhat: Before a high-stakes project, agree which requests require independent approval and how anyone can stop the process.
psychology.take: I would make refusal a supported organisational action, not a test of personal bravery.
psychology.watch: Check whether a real escalation receives a documented response without retaliation.

psychology.label: Psychology · 19 Nov 2026
psychology.headline: The wording of a question changes the answer remembered
psychology.summary: Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer’s 1974 first experiment showed accident films to 45 students. Changing the collision verb altered reported speed: the smashed wording produced higher estimates than contacted. The authors considered both response bias and altered memory representation, so this experiment alone should not be treated as proof of one mechanism.
psychology.why: Recall is reconstructed using cues supplied during questioning. An interviewer can therefore contaminate evidence while believing they are merely clarifying it.
psychology.soWhat: In customer research or an incident review, obtain an uninterrupted account before introducing your preferred explanation.
psychology.take: Preserving the interviewer’s exact question is part of preserving the evidence.
psychology.watch: Compare responses to a neutral prompt with answers obtained after a leading follow-up.

psychology.label: Psychology · 19 Nov 2026
psychology.headline: AI persuasion evidence needs its correction attached
psychology.summary: Francesco Salvi and colleagues’ 2025 study analysed 750 participants in structured online debates comparing human and GPT-4 opponents. Personalised AI was more persuasive than the human baseline. A September 2026 correction clarified that its advantage over non-personalised AI was not statistically significant; personalisation itself was therefore not conclusively isolated.
psychology.why: An experiment can support a practical concern while leaving the proposed mechanism uncertain. Model fluency, conversational responsiveness and demographic targeting should not be treated as interchangeable explanations.
psychology.soWhat: When assessing persuasive marketing tools, test incremental effects against a credible untargeted alternative.
psychology.take: Conversational influence deserves attention; stronger claims about targeting need stronger comparisons.
psychology.watch: Look for independent replications reporting preregistered comparisons and effects beyond the immediate debate.

psychology.headline: A shared human identity can widen cooperation across groups
psychology.summary: May Farid and colleagues’ 2026 randomised trial involved 8,648 young people in India. An intensive education programme emphasising identification with all humanity reduced discriminatory attitudes and behaviours and improved cross-group prosocial behaviour. The findings concern this specific programme and population, not a generic motivational slogan.
psychology.why: People can retain particular identities while broadening whom they include in a shared moral community. Training may change how differences are interpreted rather than requiring everyone to become the same.
psychology.soWhat: For team learning, pair shared goals with structured cooperation, and test workplace adaptations on their own evidence.
psychology.take: Shared identity needs practice behind it; branding alone does not demonstrate changed behaviour.
psychology.watch: Measure cooperation and fair allocation after training, then check whether improvements persist beyond the session.
